narrative:
Mara found Iven at the east gate with blood on his sleeve and the warden’s seal in his hand. The seal was hers. So was the knife lying three paces away, though the warden had not yet noticed it.

“You’re late,” Iven said.

“I was hoping you’d surrender before I had to become involved.”

His mouth tightened. “You always did prefer your rescues deniable.”

Beyond him, the gatehouse bell began to ring. The patrol had found the broken latch. If they searched Iven, they would find the ledger page tucked inside his coat—the page that proved Mara had altered the levy rolls, and that Iven had discovered her doing it. If they searched her, they would find the missing seal.

Mara held out her hand. “Give me the page.”

“Ask properly.”

“That would be an unusual burden to place on you.”

“Then offer something.”

She looked past him at the road, where the patrol’s lanterns multiplied in the rain. Iven had betrayed her once already. He would do it again if survival made the arithmetic favorable. She could not trust him. She could, perhaps, make trusting her less foolish than the alternative.

“Take the north road,” she said. “There’s a horse in the old quarry. You’ll have food until the border.”

“And you?”

“I’ll explain the seal.”

“You’ll lie.”

“I’ll explain it convincingly.”

He gave a short, humorless laugh. Then he drew the ledger page from his coat but did not surrender it. “You expect me to believe this is generosity?”

“No. I expect you to recognize a transaction.”

“What do you want?”

“Your silence until dawn.”

“And after dawn?”

“After dawn, you may hate me in public.”

For the first time, fear showed in him—not in his face, but in the way his thumb covered the ink bearing her name. He knew what the page cost her. He also knew what it would cost him to keep it.

Mara stepped toward the patrol lights. Iven caught her wrist.

“You could have left me,” he said.

“I considered it.”

“That’s not an apology.”

“No,” she said, meeting his eyes. “It’s the affordable version.”

His grip loosened. He folded the page once, twice, and placed it in her palm. Not trust. A loan with interest.

At the gate, Mara raised the warden’s seal and smiled at the approaching patrol. Behind her, Iven vanished into the rain. She heard him whistle once from the dark—the signal they had used before they became rivals.

She did not answer. But she left the gate unbarred.
title: The Price of the Gate
